primary_symptom: My loved one is making a loud gurgling or rattling sound when they breathe. Are they choking?
common_terms: choking sound, gargling, wet breathing, death rattle, fluid in lungs, noisy breathing

patient_profile.vital_concerns: Family is terrified the patient is suffocating.

recommended_interventions: First, take a deep breath. They are not choking and this does not hurt them.
This sound happens because they are deeply asleep and too weak to swallow their normal saliva.
Gently roll them onto their side. This allows gravity to pull the spit out of their mouth so the air can pass quietly.
Wipe their mouth gently with a soft cloth.
contraindications_warnings: Do not try to suck the spit out with a machine or tube; it will hurt them and make their body create even more spit.
Do not panic. It sounds much worse to you than it feels to them.
evidence_reference: Based on standard Hospice Family Education pamphlets for End-of-Life care.

condition: Panic from Not Getting Enough Air
primary_symptom: They are gasping for air, their chest is heaving, and they are panicking because they feel like they can't breathe.
common_terms: can't breathe, gasping, suffocating, panting, panic attack, chest tightness

patient_profile.vital_concerns: Severe fear and exhaustion from struggling to breathe.

recommended_interventions: Sit them up in bed and put pillows on their lap so they can lean forward and rest their arms.
Turn on a small fan and point it directly at their face. The feeling of cool wind tricks the brain into feeling like it's getting plenty of air.
If the nurse gave you a liquid pain medicine specifically for breathing (like liquid morphine), give it now. It calms the breathing center in the brain.
Hold their hand, speak softly, and ask them to match your slow breathing.
contraindications_warnings: Do not leave them alone in the room; fear makes the breathlessness much worse.
Do not force them to lie flat on their back.
evidence_reference: Based on Macmillan Cancer Support guides for managing breathlessness at home.

condition: Waking Them Up for Pain Medicine
primary_symptom: They are finally asleep, but it's time for their scheduled pain pill. Should I wake them up to give it?
common_terms: sleeping, skip pain pill, let them sleep, schedule, won't wake up

patient_profile.vital_concerns: Fear of causing an overdose vs. fear of them waking up in agony.

recommended_interventions: Yes, gently wake them up to take their scheduled, long-lasting pain medicine.
Pain medicine works best when it stays at a steady level in the body. If you let it wear off completely, they may wake up in terrible pain.
It is much harder to stop a severe pain spike than it is to prevent it from happening.
contraindications_warnings: Do not skip the main pain pills just because they look comfortable right now.
Do not give extra pills if they are too sleepy to safely swallow; call your nurse instead.
evidence_reference: Based on Hospice Foundation of America caregiver guidelines for pain management.

primary_symptom: They are pulling at their clothes, talking to people who aren't in the room, and trying to climb out of bed.
common_terms: crazy, seeing ghosts, talking to dead relatives, restless, confused, pulling blankets, won't stay in bed

patient_profile.vital_concerns: Risk of falling out of bed; family is highly distressed.

recommended_interventions: Check if they are physically uncomfortable. Do they have a full bladder? Are they constipated? Often, restlessness is the only way they can show they are in pain.
Keep the lights dim but not completely dark, and turn off the TV to reduce noise.
If they are talking to a relative who has passed away, do not argue with them or tell them it's not real. Let them find comfort in it.
If they are trying to stand up and might fall, sit right beside them and hold their hand to keep them grounded.
contraindications_warnings: Do not tie them down or hold them down by force. This will terrify them and make them fight harder.
Do not argue with their hallucinations.
evidence_reference: Based on Alzheimer's Association and Hospice guides for terminal agitation.
